sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: GraphQL interview questions test whether you understand the query-language alternative to REST — schema design (types, queries, mutations, subscriptions), resolvers, the N+1 problem and DataLoader, schema federation, persisted queries, error handling, security (depth limiting, query cost analysis), and the integration patterns with Spring for GraphQL. Expect the interviewer to compare GraphQL to REST and ask when you would choose each — that question is covered in depth here.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body:
GraphQL = **single endpoint** + **typed schema** + **client-driven queries**.

- **Resolvers** map fields to data; the resolver tree is the call graph.
- **DataLoader** batches + caches per-request — fixes the N+1.
- **Mutations** are RPC-flavoured; subscriptions are WebSocket / SSE.
- **Federation** stitches multiple subgraphs into one API.
- **Schema-first** vs code-first — pick a side and stick to it.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
The interview surface for this module breaks into these focus areas:

- **Graphql fundamentals** — drill the named patterns, the failure modes, and the recommended Java / framework idiom.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- **Over-fetching** is REST's problem; GraphQL's problem is **over-asking**.
- **Persisted queries** — security + caching + bandwidth.
- **Auth** — at the resolver level; *not* in middleware.
- **Depth / cost limits** — prevent malicious deep queries.
- **Errors** — partial-success model; clients must handle field-level errors.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: > *"I'd model the schema around the read needs of the client, batch nested fetches with DataLoader, persist queries for cacheability, enforce depth + cost limits, and authorise inside resolvers so each field is independently checked."*
